entry.title: Geometry-Aware Score-Repellent Monte Carlo

link.title: Geometry-Aware Score-Repellent Monte Carlo

entry.content:
The recently proposed Score-Repellent Monte Carlo (SRMC) method improves MCMC sampling by tilting the target density $\pi$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the factor $\exp(-\alpha\,\theta_n^\top s(x))$, where the score function $s(x) = \nabla_x \log \pi(x)$, and $\theta_n$ is the score average from past samples. However, a single scalar repellence strength $\alpha\ge0$ cannot handle both the steep and the flat directions in anisotropic energy landscapes at once. We introduce \emph{Geometry-Aware SRMC} (GA-SRMC), which generalizes the Euclidean alignment to $\theta^\top M s(x)$ for any symmetric positive-definite matrix $M$. A stochastic-approximation central limit theorem under a trace constraint on $M$ identifies the trace-normalized inverse Fisher $M_{\rm opt}\propto S^{-1}$ as the unique minimizer of the worst-direction covariance bound, elevating the Fisher information $S=\text{Cov}\pi(s,s)$ from a proposal-side preconditioner (e.g., FisherMALA, natural gradient) to the bound-optimal repulsion-side matrix, with a single online estimate $\widehat S_n$ serving both roles at no additional computational cost. The full-Fisher online metric $M_n$ converges almost surely to $M{\rm opt}$ and satisfies a CLT, providing a theoretical guarantee for the online implementation of the GA-SRMC framework. On an $8$-target simulation spanning the condition number $\kappa\in[1.3,100]$ and dimension $d\in[2,785]$, GA-SRMC dominates SRMC in ESS by $\boldsymbol{4.3\times}$ on anisotropic Gaussian ($\kappa=100$) and $\boldsymbol{6.8\times}$ on MNIST under the MALA baseline, by $\boldsymbol{16\text{–}32\%}$ on three well-conditioned logistic-regression posteriors, and by up to $\boldsymbol{+48\%}$ under FisherMALA; gains peak on the most anisotropic targets, and posterior-mean MSE is lower than with SRMC in all $16$ full-Fisher implementations.

entry.title: Guidance for Prior Change via Density Ratio Estimation

link.title: Guidance for Prior Change via Density Ratio Estimation

entry.content:
Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) serves as a vital framework for parameter inference in scientific fields where simulators involve intractable likelihoods, yet while amortized generative models offer rapid posterior estimation, they are often restricted by the specific priors used during training, thereby limiting their flexibility as prior knowledge evolves. To address this prior dependency, PriorGuide was introduced as an inference-time guidance method, but due to its intractable formulation, it relies on Gaussian approximations of the reverse transition kernel and Gaussian mixture model fitting for the prior ratio, both of which introduce systematic bias. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an unbiased test-time guidance framework that leverages Density Ratio Estimation (DRE) to learn a score guidance term, effectively decoupling the inference process from the prior training. Moreover, our framework remains agnostic to the specific density ratio estimators, making it a general and flexible framework for handling prior changes. Experimental results across multiple tasks demonstrate that our method matches or outperforms PriorGuide on C2ST and MMD in most tasks while maintaining robustness even under limited overlap between the training and target priors. Furthermore, we apply our method to Bayesian updating for parameter inference from planetary light-curve data, where it also demonstrates strong effectiveness and robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/a-chenchen/dre-based-prior-guidance .

entry.title: High-Dimensional Off-Policy Evaluation without Sample Splitting using an Onsager Correction

link.title: High-Dimensional Off-Policy Evaluation without Sample Splitting using an Onsager Correction

entry.content:
Reward models used for off-policy evaluation (OPE) are commonly selected using held-out data. When sample size and context dimension grow proportionally, the difference in test risk between models fitted on the full sample and on a fixed fraction of it need not vanish. Held-out evaluation can therefore consistently estimate the test risk of the model trained on the smaller sample, but because the relative ranking of candidate reward models can change after full-data refitting, held-out selection can be suboptimal. We develop an Onsager-corrected, target-policy-weighted criterion that estimates the full-data reward model’s out-of-sample risk under the target policy using only its training observations. This enables early stopping along the full-data gradient-descent trajectory without sample splitting. For neural networks with fixed depth and hidden width under Gaussian contexts, single-index rewards, context-dependent multi-index target policies, and known context-independent logging, we prove uniform consistency of our criterion over a fixed finite set of gradient-descent iterates and a near-oracle guarantee for the selected reward model. The same correction yields a doubly robust estimator that consistently estimates the true policy value without sample splitting, even when reward-model prediction error does not vanish. Experiments show decreasing risk-estimation error as dimension grows at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio, and improved reward-model selection relative to held-out baselines. Empirically, our correction also reduces the root mean squared error of doubly robust value estimates computed from the same data used to fit and select the reward models.

entry.title: Hurricane recovery gaps lie in reconnection, not local restart

link.title: Hurricane recovery gaps lie in reconnection, not local restart

entry.content:
Climate-intensified hurricanes disrupt urban mobility, yet whether recovery is equitable across the rural-urban gradient is unclear. Analyzing device-based mobility for Hurricanes Helene and Milton, we find local activity restarted within approximately 4.5 days in both storms, whereas reconnection to the outside world took 5 days in coastal-urban Florida but 11 in inland-rural Appalachia. The gap lies in external reconnection, not local restart, implying planners should target rural isolation.

entry.title: Hypergraph Generation via Structured Stochastic Diffusion

link.title: Hypergraph Generation via Structured Stochastic Diffusion

entry.content:
Hypergraphs model higher-order interactions, but realistic hypergraph generation remains difficult because incidence, hyperedge-size heterogeneity, and overlap structure are not faithfully captured by pairwise reductions. We propose \HEDGE, a generative model defined directly on relaxed incidence matrices via a structured stochastic diffusion. The forward process combines a hypergraph-specific two-sided heat operator with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck component, preserving structure-aware noising near the data while yielding an explicit Gaussian terminal law. Conditional on an observed hypergraph, this forward process is linear-Gaussian, so conditional means, covariances, scores, and reverse-drift targets are available in closed form. We therefore learn a permutation-equivariant state-only reverse-drift field in incidence space by regressing onto exact conditional targets, and generate samples by simulating a learned reverse-time SDE from the Gaussian base law. We establish exactness in the ideal state-only setting together with finite-horizon stability guarantees, and empirically show improved hypergraph generation quality relative to strong baselines.

entry.title: Identifying Drift, Diffusion, and Causal Structure from Temporal Snapshots

link.title: Identifying Drift, Diffusion, and Causal Structure from Temporal Snapshots

entry.content:
Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) are a fundamental tool for modelling dynamic processes, including gene regulatory networks (GRNs), contaminant transport, financial markets, and image generation. However, learning the underlying SDE from data is a challenging task, especially if individual trajectories are not observable. Motivated by burgeoning research in single-cell datasets, we present the first comprehensive approach for jointly identifying the drift and diffusion of an SDE from its temporal marginals. Assuming linear drift and additive diffusion, we show that non-identifiability can only arise if the initial distribution possesses generalized rotational symmetries. We further prove that even if this condition holds, the drift and diffusion can almost always be recovered from the marginals. Additionally, we show that the causal graph of any SDE with additive diffusion can be recovered from the identified SDE parameters. To complement this theory, we adapt entropy-regularized optimal transport to handle anisotropic diffusion and introduce APPEX (Alternating Projection Parameter Estimation from $X_0$), an iterative algorithm designed to estimate the drift, diffusion, and causal graph of an additive noise SDE, solely from temporal marginals, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated data from linear additive noise SDEs.

entry.title: Instance-Optimal Estimation with Multiple LLM Judges on a Budget

link.title: Instance-Optimal Estimation with Multiple LLM Judges on a Budget

entry.content:
Evaluating large language models increasingly relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols, but such evaluations remain costly: different judges have different prices and reliabilities, and the difficulty of each prompt-response pair can vary substantially. This raises a basic allocation question: under a fixed budget, how should one distribute evaluation queries across heterogeneous judges and instances to obtain the most accurate score estimates? We formalize this question as budgeted heteroskedastic multi-judge estimation under independent, unbiased score observations. Given $K$ prompt-response pairs and $J$ judges with known costs but unknown query-judge variances, our goal is to estimate the bounded score vector while minimizing an $\ell_p$-error. Our first contribution is to analyze the inverse-variance weighted estimator (IVWE) and to derive the oracle allocation that minimizes its leading error bound. Since this allocation depends on the unknown variances, we then address the unknown-variance setting by proposing EST-IVWE, an adaptive algorithm that constructs and uses optimistic variance estimates to stabilize the empirical allocation. We prove that EST-IVWE matches the oracle IVWE rate up to lower-order terms in the budget. Our second and central theoretical contribution is a local minimax lower bound matching the leading allocation-dependent rate, establishing asymptotic instance-optimality up to logarithmic factors. An Assouad-type construction based on local, variance-preserving perturbations yields this bound both in expectation and with constant probability. A complementary Fano-type change-of-measure argument captures the logarithmic dependence on the confidence level with a different (suboptimal) allocation geometry. Finally, we numerically validate our approach on synthetic data and resampled HelpSteer2 evaluations, demonstrating improvements over na"ive uniform allocation.

entry.title: Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts

link.title: Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts

entry.content:
Quantifying the uncertainty of forecasting models is essential to assess and mitigate the risks associated with data-driven decisions, especially in volatile domains such as electricity markets. In this paper, we propose a computationally efficient isotonic variant of Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA), called Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging (iQRA), for generating probabilistic forecasts from ensembles of point forecasts. Building on QRA, we introduce stochastic order constraints as a hyperparameter-free regularization mechanism that reduces computational complexity while maintaining competitive forecast accuracy. We further demonstrate that the same isotonic regularization principle can be applied to the smoothed estimator of QRA. In an extensive forecasting study of two European day-ahead electricity markets, we show that iQRA and its smoothed variant consistently rank among the top state-of-the-art postprocessing methods in terms of reliability and sharpness. It produces well-calibrated prediction intervals, with smoothed iQRA providing superior reliability even when compared against coverage-oriented conformal prediction. We further introduce a battery arbitrage evaluation, showing that the leading probabilistic methods achieve the highest profit per trade and that probabilistic risk control improves the economic value of trading decisions. Isotonic regularization offers a scalable hyperparameter-free variable selection for linear quantile regression, making iQRA attractive for practical decision-support systems in energy markets.

entry.title: Kernel-Based Learning of Analytic Operators and Parametric PDEs

link.title: Kernel-Based Learning of Analytic Operators and Parametric PDEs

entry.content:
We study kernel-based learning of analytic operators from finite samples, with a focus on how the regularity of the target should determine the choice of the kernel. We establish embeddings of analytic operators into vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and derive finite-sample, high-probability guarantees that quantify the uncertainty due to random sampling: in the noiseless setting, suitable analytic kernels yield rates exponential in a fractional power of the sample size, while Sobolev-type kernels yield polynomial rates. We apply the theory to the solution operator of a parametric elliptic PDE, where the training data are themselves finite-element approximations, and obtain bounds that separate the sampling and discretization contributions to the error and prescribe how the mesh size should be coupled to the sample size. The results are illustrated numerically.

entry.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents

link.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents

entry.content:
Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent’s trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent’s current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent’s future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.

entry.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms

link.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms

entry.content:
We consider linear stochastic bandits where the set of actions is an ellipsoid. We provide the first known minimax optimal algorithm for this problem. We first derive a novel information-theoretic lower bound on the regret of any algorithm, which must be at least $\Omega(\min(d \sigma \sqrt{T} + d |\theta|{A}, |\theta|{A} T))$ where $d$ is the dimension, $T$ the time horizon, $\sigma^2$ the noise variance, $A$ a matrix defining the set of actions and $\theta$ the vector of unknown parameters. We then provide an algorithm whose regret matches this bound to a multiplicative universal constant. The algorithm is non-classical in the sense that it is not optimistic, and it is not a sampling algorithm. The main idea is to combine a novel sequential procedure to estimate $|\theta|$, followed by an explore-and-commit strategy informed by this estimate. The algorithm is highly computationally efficient, and a run requires only time $O(dT + d^2 \log(T/d) + d^3)$ and memory $O(d^2)$, in contrast with known optimistic algorithms, which are not implementable in polynomial time. We go beyond minimax optimality and show that our algorithm is locally asymptotically minimax optimal, a much stronger notion of optimality. We further provide numerical experiments to illustrate our theoretical findings.

entry.title: Local Inference for High-dimensional Time Series

link.title: Local Inference for High-dimensional Time Series

entry.content:
Local stationarity provides a natural framework for time series whose dependence structure evolves smoothly over time. In high-dimensional settings, however, its classical definition can break down, as approximation errors accumulate across time-varying coefficients. To address this limitation, we introduce $(\epsilon_n,\delta)$-stationarity, a generalization of local stationarity that holds locally in time and allows approximation errors to grow with the dimension, and we combine it with local sparsity, which lets the set of relevant predictors change over time. We show that, for high-dimensional time-varying autoregressions, the rate of stationary approximation is driven by local sparsity, so that local sparsity governs not only estimation but also the stationary approximation itself. We then develop a \textit{local lasso} with time-varying penalties that selects relevant predictors and their periods of activity, and we derive error bounds that depend on the local sparsity, quantify the cost of nonstationarity, and guide penalty and bandwidth selection. For inference, we propose a desparsified local lasso based on local nodewise regressions and establish a linear representation with an explicit smoothing bias. Asymptotic normality then follows under two bandwidth conditions, one for coefficient variation and one for nonstationarity. Simulations and applications to macroeconomic and neuroscience data illustrate the methods.

link.title: Locally Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Polynomial Chaos Expansions

entry.content:
This work develops a locally adaptive jackknife+ conformal prediction framework for polynomial chaos expansions. Therein, the non-conformity scores are normalized with an auxiliary polynomial chaos expansion trained on the log-transformed leave-one-out residuals of the base model. We show that the coverage guarantee of jackknife+ conformal prediction carries over to the adaptive intervals if the leave-one-out auxiliary models are trained on nested leave-one-out residuals. For fixed-basis polynomial chaos expansions fitted by ordinary least squares, all required quantities are derived in closed form and the guarantee-preserving adaptive intervals are obtained from a single model fit, without any model retraining. For sparse polynomial chaos expansions, where multiple model fits are necessary, we propose a heuristic simplification that limits the computational overhead of adaptivity at the cost of the formal coverage guarantee. Numerical experiments on an academic benchmark with known heteroscedastic noise and on an engineering simulation dataset show that the suggested method attains the target coverage while providing intervals that adapt to local prediction uncertainty, therefore being considerably more statistically efficient. These advantages are particularly prominent in high-uncertainty regions of the input space, where the performance of non-adaptive methods degrades substantially.

entry.content:
Dimensionality reduction is widely used to visualize high-dimensional data and guide scientific discovery, yet interpreting which original features contribute to low-dimensional representations remains challenging, particularly for black-box methods such as t-SNE and UMAP. We introduce \textbf{MEDALLION} (Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON), a novel framework for interpreting low-dimensional embeddings through knowledge distillation and neural feature attribution. MEDALLION distills any given embedding with a neural encoder which we explain via a broad range of existing neural feature attribution methods. Through experiments on MNIST and applications in single-cell transcriptomics, we show MEDALLION provides informative feature attributions that cast additional insights into the underlying embedding and compare its performance with existing interpretability approaches.

entry.title: M-Estimation in Censored Regression Model under Endogeneity

link.title: M-Estimation in Censored Regression Model under Endogeneity

entry.content:
This paper develops a general M-estimation framework for censored regression models under endogeneity. A two-stage estimation is proposed to address the issue of endogeneity in the first stage and the issue of censoring in linear regression models in the second stage. The issue of endogeneity is addressed via instrumental variables using the control function approach. The issue of censoring in linear regression models is addressed via M-estimation using a suitably defined class of loss functions yielding a class of estimators. Thus, the proposed general M-estimation framework nests several existing estimators as special cases for the respective loss functions. Moreover, this provides flexibility of accommodating a broad range of robust loss functions that have not previously been studied in the context of censored regression. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality for the proposed class of estimators. An empirical study based on simulated datasets is conducted to illustrate general M-estimation for various choices of loss functions and to examine the finite-sample performance of various resulting estimators.

entry.title: Machine Learning Beyond Statistical Consistency for Hybrid AI

link.title: Machine Learning Beyond Statistical Consistency for Hybrid AI

entry.content:
We propose a new definition of machine learning, according to which a machine learns a function when it computes the function successfully, that is, when the value it returns for each input has a proper derivation in a formal system. We extend G"odel’s Representability Theorem, which equates computation with derivation, to empirical targets in two ways: the theorem is extended to the computable reals, and the data are admitted into the system as empirical definitions that record what has been observed. We prove that a machine learns a true probability if and only if two conditions are met. The Truth Condition is that its estimate converges to the true probability, which is statistical consistency. The Assurance Condition is that the machine properly derives its own convergence inside the system. Learning thus lies beyond statistical consistency, for it requires a derivation of the convergence from the record. A global assumption about the data, such as the i.i.d. assumption, does not supply such a derivation, because it leads only to a circular one, as we show for PAC learning. On the other hand, the two conditions are met for the probability of a sentence over a finite ideal corpus. A real machine can approximate a true probability only if an ideal machine can learn it precisely, that is, only in a domain that meets the two conditions. Modern AI works in such a domain, and we offer this as a clue to its success. Modern AI is hybrid as well, in two senses: First, it performs two kinds of tasks, namely probabilistic ones such as predicting the next word and deductive ones such as proving and coding. Second, it combines two parts of different kinds, a statistical proposer and a deductive verifier, for proving and coding. Our framework explains both senses of hybridity in one formal system.

entry.title: Marginal-Nonuniform Multiclass Learning

link.title: Marginal-Nonuniform Multiclass Learning

entry.content:
We study the problem of multiclass classification within the framework of marginal-nonuniform learning, where the constants in the learning rate may depend on the unknown marginal distribution generating the unlabeled data, but not on the target concept. This notion naturally lies between classical PAC learning, where the constants are independent of both the marginal distribution and the target concept, and more recent universal learning, where the constants may depend on both. We give a complete characterization of the optimal marginal-nonuniform learning rates, establishing a fundamental trichotomy: exponential, linear, and arbitrarily slow rates. This characterization is witnessed by a new combinatorial dimension, termed the uncentered DS-eluder dimension. A key ingredient in the upper-bound proofs is a set of new distributional exhaustion lemmas that exploit the sequential nature of this dimension and may be of independent interest.

entry.title: Matrix Factorization Framework for Community Detection under the Degree-Corrected Block Model

link.title: Matrix Factorization Framework for Community Detection under the Degree-Corrected Block Model

entry.content:
Community detection is a fundamental task in data analysis, and block models provide an approach for identifying diverse community structures. The degree-corrected block model (DCBM) is an established model that captures node degree heterogeneity. However, inference methods are computationally costly and sensitive to initialization, while cheaper alternatives, such as spectral or modularity-based approaches, may be less effective at recovering certain non-assortative structures. In this work, we show that DCBM inference can be reformulated as a constrained nonnegative matrix trifactorization problem. Leveraging this insight, we propose a scalable community detection method with a theoretically grounded initialization providing an initial partition for inference algorithms. Our approach is agnostic to network structure and applies to any graph representable by a DCBM. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmark networks show that our method achieves community recovery comparable to, and sometimes better than, that achieved by the DCBM inference methods, while being faster: it processes a graph with 100,000 nodes and 500,000 edges in about 30 seconds. Moreover, the initialization significantly improves solution quality. Overall, this work provides a scalable and robust framework for community detection and highlights the benefits of a matrix-factorization perspective for the DCBM.

entry.title: Measuring and Decomposing Mode Separation via the Canonical Diffusion

link.title: Measuring and Decomposing Mode Separation via the Canonical Diffusion

entry.content:
Mode separation, namely how sharply a distribution fragments into barrier-separated clusters, is a fundamental geometric property of densities, difficult to quantify in high dimensions. Modes are often the meaningful alternatives in the data, such as the conformations of a molecule or the distinct semantic types among a generative model’s outputs. Mode separation is distinct from dispersion, which is what standard label-free tools capture: differential entropy rises with spread regardless of fragmentation, and PCA orders directions by variance regardless of barriers. Mutual information does capture it, but only given the latent component labels, which are usually unavailable. We measure mode separation through a single stochastic process intrinsic to the density, namely the unique reversible diffusion with $f$ as its stationary distribution and a constant scalar diffusion coefficient. From its autocovariance matrix we extract two readouts. The first, SSA (Sum of Squared Autocorrelations), is a scalar barrier-sensitive measure. The second, DA (Dominant Autocorrelation directions), gives linear projections ordered by metastability rather than variance. Under an isotropic-Gaussian null, we derive the limiting spectrum of the empirical autocovariance in closed form, generalizing the Marchenko–Pastur law. Its upper edge gives a noise floor that separates metastable directions from sampling noise. Both readouts use only samples and a score function, scaling to high dimensions through pretrained score-based generative models via Tweedie’s identity. We apply our framework to three settings: (i) synthetic Gaussian mixtures, where SSA tracks mutual information; (ii) SDXL text-to-image generations, where SSA and DA capture structure that entropy and PCA miss; and (iii) molecular dynamics of alanine dipeptide, where DA recovers the known slow backbone dihedrals from static samples alone.

entry.title: Minimax designs and estimators for causal inference under network interference

link.title: Minimax designs and estimators for causal inference under network interference

entry.content:
We develop a design-based minimax theory for linear causal estimands under interference. We study the minimax risks of three problems: optimizing an estimator under a fixed design, optimizing an estimator and a design from a restricted class, or optimizing both over all designs. In each problem, we study the minimax risk over all estimators and over design-unbiased estimators separately. We allow any correctly specified exposure mapping, including the identity. Our theory represents causal inference under interference as a constrained sampling design on an expanded finite population of $\sum_i d_i$ potential outcomes, where $d_i$ is the number of exposure levels attainable by unit $i$. We describe the constrained sampling design by a weighted sampling hypergraph: its vertices are the potential outcomes, its hyperedges are the maximal sets of potential outcomes that can be jointly sampled under feasible treatment assignments, and its weights are induced by the randomization design. We show that the minimax risks of the fixed-design, restricted-design, and all-design problems depend, respectively, on the weighted hypergraph induced by the design, the collection of weighted hypergraphs attainable within the restricted class, and the unweighted hypergraph. Our Bayes lower bounds compare potential-outcome tables that differ on jointly missing sets of potential outcomes: joint-missingness probabilities govern the lower bounds over all estimators, whereas the corresponding odds govern the lower bounds over unbiased estimators. We illustrate the theory for average treatment effects without interference, saturation designs under partial interference, total, direct, and contagion effects under neighborhood interference, and bipartite dose-response contrasts. The upper and lower bounds match in several settings.

entry.title: Model-Agnostic FDR Control via Group Gaussian Mirror and Permutation SHAP

link.title: Model-Agnostic FDR Control via Group Gaussian Mirror and Permutation SHAP

entry.content:
Most FDR-controlled feature selection methods are designed for coordinate-wise hypotheses, where each feature has a single weight or importance score. This abstraction fails in sequential and grouped models, where one original feature is represented by a block of sub-features, such as lags, recurrent states, or attention-based interactions. We propose a grouped-feature FDR control framework for such settings. For grouped linear models, we construct null-symmetric block-level mirror statistics with matrix-valued perturbations. For neural sequential models, we combine Permutation SHAP derivatives as model-agnostic block-level importance scores with kernel-based dependence measure. The framework is model-agnostic across network architectures, does not require specifying the covariate distribution, and reduces to Gaussian Mirror or Neural Gaussian Mirror when the block size is one. We prove FDR control for low- and high-dimensional grouped linear models and asymptotic symmetry of smoothed Permutation SHAP derivatives under fixed fitted nonlinear models. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets show reliable FDR control and improved power under correlated grouped-feature signals.

entry.title: Multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression for noisy outputs and non-nested experimental designs: decoupled versus joint likelihood optimization

link.title: Multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression for noisy outputs and non-nested experimental designs: decoupled versus joint likelihood optimization

entry.content:
This paper investigates a recursive formulation of auto-regressive multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression in the challenging setting of noisy and non-nested high- and low-fidelity data. We propose a decoupled optimization strategy based on the expectation-maximization algorithm, which exploits the structure of the recursive model. In particular, we derive closed-form update formulas when the scaling factor is modeled as a parametric linear predictor. This approach is compared with the fully coupled likelihood maximization of the classical, non-recursive formulation. A series of benchmark experiments, covering applications of increasing complexity, highlights the performance of both approaches. The results demonstrate that the proposed recursive strategy substantially reduces training time when large low-fidelity datasets are available, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation.

entry.title: Multi-layer dissolution exponential-family models for weighted signed networks

link.title: Multi-layer dissolution exponential-family models for weighted signed networks

entry.content:
Understanding the structure of signed weighted networks is essential for analysing complex systems in which relationships between nodes vary both in sign and strength. Despite significant advances in statistical network analysis, there is still a lack of models that can account for both the sign and the strength of interactions in networks. We introduce a multi-layer dissolution exponential random graph modelling framework that enables systematic assessment of structural balance effects. We adopt a fully-probabilistic hierarchical approach that partially pools information across layers, with parameters estimated via an adaptive approximate exchange algorithm. A simulation study shows that the algorithm recovers the layer-specific parameters with small bias. We demonstrate the flexibility and explanatory power of the proposed methodology through an application to the gene interaction network associated with dilated cardiomyopathy, in which a multi-layer signed structure is constructed by progressively thresholding interaction confidence scores, with edge signs derived from pairwise co-expression. The analysis shows that positive co-expression edges embedded in positive triangles are more likely to persist at higher confidence levels, while negative edges whose endpoints share positive partners, which form unbalanced triangles, are preferentially dissolved as the confidence threshold increases.

entry.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)

link.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)

entry.content:
Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite this broad potential impact, selection bias is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct it, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle and assumptions, and we compare methods addressing the same form of selection by their assumptions, data requirements and limitations. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R, prepares input for the external SPREG software, and provides worked examples on simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection, one of which we present in full. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with recommendations for bias-aware study design, sensitivity analysis and reporting.

entry.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning

link.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning

entry.content:
Multi-agent language systems are often built as hand-designed workflows, where agents are assigned semantic roles and communication protocols are specified in advance. We propose NeuroMAS, a framework that treats a multi-agent language system as a trainable and scalable neural-network-like architecture with hidden textual intermediate signals. In NeuroMAS, language-agent nodes are role-free but structure-aware: the topology determines how information can flow, while reward-based training determines how nodes communicate, specialize, and coordinate. This formulation shifts multi-agent design from workflow engineering toward architecture design, where depth, width, connectivity, and growth protocol become scalable sources of capability. We provide a theoretical perspective showing why such modular text-valued computation can be parameter-efficient when tasks admit stable decompositions. Experiments show that NeuroMAS improves over both inference-time collaboration methods and trained baselines, and that its gains are not explained by trainable parameter count alone. We further find that organizational scaling is path-dependent: larger systems can fail when trained from scratch, but become stronger when grown progressively from smaller trained systems. These results suggest that learned multi-agent organization is a promising scaling axis for language-model reasoning and generation.

entry.title: New optimisations for exact, scalable 2D Gaussian process inference, with applications to astronomical time-series

link.title: New optimisations for exact, scalable 2D Gaussian process inference, with applications to astronomical time-series

entry.content:
Astronomical datasets often consist of a grid of datapoints in two or more dimensions, such as images, spectroscopic time-series, and imaging time-series. Gaussian processes (GPs) are a powerful tool for dealing with correlated noise in these data, arising from both astrophysical and instrumental systematics. Despite this, popular GP optimisations such as celerite are largely restricted to 1D datasets. Extensions to 2D data typically come with limited flexibility or poor scaling. As a motivating example, this limitation is significant for transiting exoplanet spectroscopy with JWST, as current analyses typically assume each spectroscopic light curve is statistically independent, despite many potential sources of wavelength-correlation, including detector readout noise and stellar granulation. This introduces a potential bias in atmospheric retrievals which is typically ignored. To solve this problem, we present new, exact GP optimisations implemented in the JAX-based package luas, which extend 1D GP optimisations to multidimensional data using Kronecker product algebra. These GP optimisations are highly flexible, permit efficient analysis of 2D datasets containing millions of datapoints, and in many cases have a cheaper cost than transit light curve modelling. These optimisations are key to pushing the limits of exoplanet spectroscopy to smaller targets around bright host stars, as we increasingly hit instrumental and astrophysical noise floors. We suggest further applications to the analysis of ground-based high resolution spectroscopic time-series, extreme precision radial velocities, and high-contrast imaging, drawing on the connection that certain 2D GP models represent a probabilistic generalisation of PCA. Applications may even extend to machine learning and geostatistics, as we present novel optimisations for the Linear Mixing Model and the Linear Model of Coregionalisation.

entry.title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness

link.title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness

entry.content:
Can a network look stable at every layer and still be exponentially unstable as a whole? The Lipschitz constant of a neural network is a basic stability quantity appearing in optimization guarantees, generalization bounds, and robustness certificates. Deep networks naturally admit two such notions, input Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to data perturbations, and parameter Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to weight perturbations. We prove that, for deep networks with normalization layers, with batch normalization as the canonical example, both Lipschitz constants can grow exponentially with depth and hence with parameter dimension, even under strong per-layer norm control such as $|W_\ell|_2\le 1$, and already for linear activations. Thus, a mechanism widely used to stabilize training can create severe worst-case instabilities that are invisible locally, i.e., from layerwise norm bounds alone. Parameter-Lipschitz explosion turns Lipschitz-dependent nonsmooth optimization guarantees into exponential-in-dimension bounds for deep normalized networks, while input-Lipschitz explosion makes worst-case Lipschitz-based generalization and robustness certificates vacuous. The latter also yields a concrete rank-separation mechanism for adversarial vulnerability. The theory predicts that perturbations introducing new singular directions should be amplified much more strongly than perturbations at the same noise level that remain within the input’s original singular subspace. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support this prediction, showing that rank-creating perturbations cause substantially sharper drops in accuracy, confidence, and margins than same-subspace perturbations.

link.title: Online Causal Configuration for Networked Systems via Doubly Robust Steady-State Learning

entry.content:
Measurement exploration reveals how interacting local controllers behave but can alter the steady-state regime a network operator seeks to optimize. Exploratory rewards may therefore fail to identify a configuration’s no-exploration value: under full exploration, identical logged distributions can conceal different target values. Identification requires accounting for both action-law mismatch and shifts in the steady-state context distribution. We introduce CAUSAL-UCB, which selects configurations using optimistic bounds on target causal values. Its interference-aware clipped doubly robust evaluator produces predecision certificates separating statistical variation from calibrated identification, transport, and temporal-dependence errors. For any finite horizon and predetermined schedule of measurement-exploration rates ${\eta_t}$, we prove lower bounds of $\Omega((1+\sum_t\eta_t)^{-1/2})$ on minimax inference error and $\Omega(\sum_t\eta_t)$ on measurement-induced deployment loss in a stationary, potentially slow-mixing family. We bound regret under valid certificates and selected-information growth, and establish an anytime finite-sample certificate with a shared radius for estimation, selection, and reporting in a restricted known-local-interference model. In a high-mismatch benchmark with 24 paired seeds and 200 rounds, CAUSAL-UCB attains target regret of $1.732$ versus $6.326$ for certified IPS-UCB, with deployment gaps of $30.607$ and $23.217$, respectively. Independent-audit coverage tests and trace-driven semi-synthetic studies further assess certificate coverage and deployment trade-offs.

link.title: Online and Survey Representations of Well-Being: Coherence and Cross-Source Correspondence

entry.content:
Digital traces may complement population surveys in the measurement of well-being, but the two sources do not necessarily capture identical constructs. We compare the Human Flourishing Geographic Index (HFGI) with World Values Survey and European Social Survey measures across three domains using structural equation models. The results show strong within-source coherence and construct-specific cross-source correspondence. entry.title: Optimal Forecast Reconciliation with Uncertainty Quantification

link.title: Optimal Forecast Reconciliation with Uncertainty Quantification

entry.content:
We propose to estimate the weight matrix used for forecast reconciliation as parameters in a general linear model in order to quantify its uncertainty. This implies that forecast reconciliation can be formulated as an orthogonal projection from the space of base-forecast errors into a coherent linear subspace. We use variance decomposition together with the Wishart distribution to derive the central estimator for the forecast-error covariance matrix. In addition, we prove that distance-reducing properties apply to the reconciled forecasts at all levels of the hierarchy as well as to the forecast-error covariance. A covariance matrix for the reconciliation weight matrix is derived, which leads to improved estimates of the forecast-error covariance matrix. We show how shrinkage can be introduced in the formulated model by imposing specific priors on the weight matrix and the forecast-error covariance matrix. The method is illustrated in a simulation study that shows consistent improvements in the log-score. Finally, standard errors for the weight matrix and the variance-separation formula are illustrated using a case study of forecasting electricity load in Sweden.

link.title: Optimal In-context Adaptivity and Distributional Robustness of Transformers

entry.content:
We study in-context learning problems where a Transformer is pretrained on tasks drawn from a mixture distribution $\pi=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}} \lambda_{\alpha} \pi_{\alpha}$, called the pretraining prior, in which each mixture component $\pi_{\alpha}$ is a distribution on tasks of a specific difficulty level indexed by $\alpha$. Our goal is to understand the performance of the pretrained Transformer when evaluated on a different test distribution $\mu$, consisting of tasks of fixed difficulty $\beta\in\mathcal{A}$, and with potential distribution shift relative to $\pi_\beta$, subject to the chi-squared divergence $\chi^2(\mu,\pi_{\beta})$ being at most $\kappa$. In particular, we consider nonparametric regression problems with random smoothness, and multi-index models with both random smoothness and random effective dimension. Thus, the pretrained Transformer is able to achieve faster rates of convergence on easier tasks and is robust to distribution shift at test time. Finally, we prove that even if an estimator had access to the test distribution $\mu$, the convergence rate of its expected risk over $\mu$ could not be faster than that of our pretrained Transformers, thereby providing a more appropriate optimality guarantee than minimax lower bounds.

entry.title: Optimizing Computational-Statistical Runtime for Wasserstein Distance Estimation

link.title: Optimizing Computational-Statistical Runtime for Wasserstein Distance Estimation

entry.content:
Squared Wasserstein distance is a frequently used tool to measure discrepancy between probability distributions. This distance is typically computed between empirical measures of size $n$ from two underlying random samples. Unfortunately, even in lower dimensional Euclidean space problems $\left( d \in {2,3} \right)$, algorithms for Wasserstein distance computation with approximate or exact precision guarantees scale poorly in the runtime as a function of $n$ and the desired precision. In response, we consider the computational-statistical runtime, where the goal is to estimate from samples the Wasserstein distance between potentially smooth measures up to $\epsilon$-additive error in expectation with respect to the sampling; we allow $O(1)$ computational cost for collecting a sample. Towards this, we develop a Sample-Sketch-Solve paradigm where we introduce a regular cartesian grid sketch of the samples. We show that (especially under $\alpha$-H"older smooth distributions) this can compress the data without increasing asymptotic error, and also regularizes the structure which enables faster exact algorithms. Ultimately, we approximate $W_2^2(P,Q)$ within $\epsilon$ error in $\epsilon^{-\max(2,\frac{d+1+o(1)}{1+\alpha})}$ time for $0 < \alpha < 1$ H"older smooth distributions $P,Q$ on $(0,1)^{d}$; an optimal $\Theta(\epsilon^{-2})$ for $\alpha > 1/2$ when $d=2$ and nearly optimal as $\alpha \to 1$ when $d = 3$.

entry.title: Ordered Policy Optimization

link.title: Ordered Policy Optimization

entry.content:
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.

entry.title: Outlier-Robust Multi-Output Gaussian Processes

link.title: Outlier-Robust Multi-Output Gaussian Processes

entry.content:
Multi-output Gaussian process (MOGP) regression allows modelling dependencies among multiple correlated response variables. Similarly to standard Gaussian processes (GPs), MOGPs are sensitive to model misspecification and outliers, which can distort predictions within individual outputs. In the multi-output case, this situation can be further exacerbated as anomalous observations in one response can adversely influence predictions for other correlated outputs. To handle this situation, we propose R-MOGP, an MOGP that is provably robust to outliers in any individual response. Our approach preserves conjugacy, achieving robustness without sacrificing computational efficiency, and integrates naturally with sparse variational inference for scalability. Empirically, we show that R-MOGP achieves performance comparable to existing state-of-the-art robust MOGPs at a fraction of their computational costs.

entry.title: Portfolio-aware scenario transfer of reserve movements: evidence from Lloyd’s syndicates

link.title: Portfolio-aware scenario transfer of reserve movements: evidence from Lloyd’s syndicates

entry.content:
A claims-development movement on one portfolio may not transfer directly as a stress to another size. We estimate how to transfer such scenarios between portfolio sizes, using 632 syndicate-years from 117 Lloyd’s syndicates over 2015-2024. The measured movement is the change in gross claims estimates on selected older underwriting cohorts, divided by opening gross claims outstanding plus reserves taken on in the year whose development it includes; it is not a pure measure of opening-reserve deterioration. Its dispersion falls materially with reserve size, and a size-based scale predicts held-out syndicates far better than a single market scale. But the transferred upper tail understates the smallest books: in the smallest reserve-size quartile, six of 158 held-out observations exceeded the transferred 99.5th percentile, against 0.79 expected, from three syndicates. Square-root scaling has descriptively lower held-out pinball loss at 99% and 99.5%, though more misses among the largest books. For a GBP 500m portfolio the transferred empirical 99.5th percentile is 0.34 of reserves (95% credible interval, conditional on the fitted model, 0.23-0.52), against 0.67 in the raw market pool. Both are Syndicate 5820’s 2016 movement. The contribution is inspectable scenario comparability, not a calibrated capital quantile or a next-year forecast.

entry.title: Power improvements and exact shortcuts for closed permutation maxT testing with discrete data

link.title: Power improvements and exact shortcuts for closed permutation maxT testing with discrete data

entry.content:
In permutation tests with discrete data, especially in small samples, different permutations often yield the same test statistic. The resulting ties can make the test conservative and reduce power. This conservatism can be particularly pronounced for maximum statistics: permutations may have the same maximum but differ at other endpoints, so the remaining endpoint statistics are discarded. We develop two power improvements for closed permutation maxT tests by refining the treatment of ties. The first method uses a single uniform random variable shared across all local tests in the closed testing procedure. This shared-uniform construction maximizes the rejection probability of every elementary hypothesis among all ways of coordinating the same randomized local tests. It also preserves an exact linear step-down shortcut. The second method is the deterministic two-endpoint augmentation (tea) test, which uses the second-largest endpoint statistic to resolve ties in the maximum. This additional information can favour rejection under alternatives while preserving null validity, without auxiliary randomization. Its full closure admits an exact quadratic shortcut. More generally, augmentation using any fixed number of endpoint statistics admits an exact polynomial shortcut. Both procedures retain every rejection made by classical closed maxT procedures and provide strong finite-sample control of the family-wise error rate under intersection-null permutation invariance. In simulations with sparse binary outcomes, both methods improve power over classical closed maxT testing. When many endpoints are tested, the tea test also often outperforms shared-uniform randomization.

entry.title: Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation for a Genuinely Unbalanced Dynamic Network Panel Data Model

link.title: Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation for a Genuinely Unbalanced Dynamic Network Panel Data Model

entry.content:
This paper develops quasi-maximum likelihood estimation for genuinely unbalanced dynamic network panel data models. We first study a baseline one-way fixed effect specification and then extend the framework to two-way fixed effects. The model accommodates contemporaneous and lagged network spillovers, temporal dependence, and a listing effect that operates when a unit first appears in the panel. For the baseline specification, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the QMLE, characterize the incidental-parameter bias, and propose a bias-corrected estimator. We further provide a consistent estimator of the asymptotic covariance matrix, to enable feasible inference. Under the two-way fixed effect extension, we derive the corresponding asymptotic distribution, bias correction, and covariance matrix estimator, accounting for the additional bias component induced by the time fixed effects. Monte Carlo simulations examine the finite sample performance of the proposed estimators and inference procedure. An empirical application to Airbnb listings from New Zealand and New York City reveals region-specific patterns in spatial and temporal price transmission, highlighting the importance of modeling genuine unbalancedness in dynamic network settings.

entry.title: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs

link.title: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs

entry.content:
We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be computationally hard in this setting, so prior work has explored natural assumptions that make planning easier. Recent work [Golowich et al., 2022] gave quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for observable POMDPs. These are POMDPs whose observation channels satisfy an $\ell_1$-observability condition, but notably, no assumptions are required on the transition dynamics. In a similar vein, for every fixed $\rho>0$, we give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for $\rho$-decodable POMDPs. We show that decodability is implied by both $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. Moreover, we show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal $\ell_1$-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. We also show that the fast filter-forgetting guarantee underlying the approach of [Golowich et al., 2022] does not extend directly from $\ell_1$-observability to constant $\ell_2$-observability. Thus, decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.

entry.title: Replication Certification at Publication: Checkable by Anyone, Anywhere, in Seconds, Forever

link.title: Replication Certification at Publication: Checkable by Anyone, Anywhere, in Seconds, Forever

entry.content:
Authors increasingly deposit replication datasets—the data and code behind publications—in archives, and journals increasingly require them to, under progressively onerous rules. But a deposit alone proves little, so authors keep paying: months for the journal’s reanalyses, years answering readers’ questions, and rancor as failed replications become accusations because no record establishes what actually ran. We introduce a replication certificate: a cryptographically signed record of the deposited files and logged output. It replaces the journal’s reanalyses with evidence anyone can check in seconds, which no one, including the archive, can backdate, and no one can fake without risking detection. Certification asks little of anyone and benefits everyone: The author deposits, then reruns the analysis once under a random seed the archive computes from the deposit’s hash and a blockchain block; the archive signs, timestamps (in that blockchain), and stores the record—confidential data included—without rerunning anything; the journal merely checks a website for the certificate; and anyone can check or replay any step decades later.

link.title: Response-guided knockoffs for prespecified directional FDR control in linear models

entry.content:
Conventional false discovery rate (FDR) control limits the expected proportion of selected features that are unrelated to the response. Directional FDR extends this criterion to also account for incorrect sign estimates. In some applications, however, discoveries are sought only in a direction specified in advance. We therefore introduce the prespecified directional FDR, which counts as errors both null effects and effects opposite to the target direction in context of the fixed-design Gaussian linear model with unknown noise variance. A straightforward adaptation of the knockoff filter provides prespecified directional FDR control. To improve power, we develop the response-guided knockoff filter, which uses a noise-perturbed response to guide knockoff construction in favour of features likely to have the target sign, while retaining finite-sample prespecified directional FDR control. Notably, our improved filter maintains this guarantee with a sample size $n>p+2$ in contrast to standard constructions that require $n\geq2p$. Simulations across a range of settings demonstrate power gains of the response-guided knockoff filter. An application to HIV drug-resistance data illustrates improved recovery of externally annotated resistance-associated mutations.

link.title: Reweighting for Transfer Classification: Exact Risk Conversion and Minimax Adaptation

entry.content:
A source can make a training mixture easier to learn while making its accuracy less valuable for the target. We study how the training problem a source creates and the finite-sample error of learning it jointly determine target-risk guarantees under reweighting. For binary classification, for each pair of laws and each positive target weight, we derive the sharpest target excess hinge-risk bound implied by mixture excess alone, uniformly over clipped predictors. This exact conversion curve is determined by density-weighted local votes. A two-sample oracle inequality for weighted support vector machines supplies the mixture excess, and the composition becomes explicit for Gaussian kernels. On a tilted-boundary class, we establish the all-procedure minimax classification rate $[n+s_+^2/(m^{-1}+\tau^2)]^{-1}$ in the transferable strength $s_+$ and the tilt $\tau$, separating source sampling uncertainty ($m^{-1}$) from relation uncertainty ($\tau^2$). A target-checked Gaussian-SVM selector adapts to unknown $s_+$ and $\tau$ up to a logarithmic factor for fixed dimension, and retains the target-only rate up to the same factor against arbitrary independent sources under the stated target model. On a separate smooth opposition class, the minimax risk within the family of exact Gaussian SVMs fitted to the original labels with nonnegative weights is exponentially larger than the unrestricted minimax risk whenever the target sample is at most half the source sample, despite arbitrary data-dependent weighting and tuning. The value of a source thus depends on the training problem it creates, on what accuracy there means for the target, and on whether the permitted use of the source can implement the needed correction.

link.title: Risk-set reconstruction balance: zero-targeted diagnostics for artificial censoring in clone-censor-weight analyses

entry.content:
In clone-censor-weight (CCW) analyses, inverse probability of censoring weighting corrects selection from artificial censoring at protocol deviation. Balance diagnostics, such as the end-of-grace between-strategy standardised mean difference (SMD) and censoring balance, compare different populations, and their zero targets under a correct model are not formally stated. We show that, under positivity and a correct censoring model, the weighted retained individuals reconstruct the risk set before each censoring interval and the baseline population, and we propose risk-set reconstruction balance (RRB), which measures how far they depart from these two populations. Interval RRB has a zero target for every history function, including post-baseline covariates, for which between-strategy SMDs have none. entry.title: Robust Ensemble Kalman Filtering Under Observation Noise Misspecification

link.title: Robust Ensemble Kalman Filtering Under Observation Noise Misspecification

entry.content:
We address observation noise misspecification in Bayesian filtering of dynamical systems via generalised Bayesian inference. Mismatch in tail decay between the true data generating process and an assumed observation model, often indicated via outliers, can strongly impact Bayesian updates in Kalman filters and their ensemble approximations. Adjusting information processing in the analysis step by employing diffusion score matching achieves robustness while maintaining closed-form Gaussian updates and good uncertainty quantification. We provide theoretical properties of this novel Kalman filter in linear Gaussian state space systems covering conjugacy of the analysis step, robustness, covariance stability, and tuning. We extend the approach to non-linear signal dynamics by adapting ensemble Kalman filter variants. Simulation studies on 2D target tracking and the Lorenz-63 and 40D Lorenz-96 systems highlight a critical trade-off between robustness and stability in filtering.

entry.title: Robust Multimodal Learning via Entropy-Gated Contrastive Fusion

link.title: Robust Multimodal Learning via Entropy-Gated Contrastive Fusion

entry.content:
Real-world multimodal systems routinely face missing-input scenarios, and in reality, robots lose audio in a factory or a clinical record omits lab tests at inference time. Standard fusion layers either preserve robustness or calibration but never both. We introduce Adaptive Entropy-Gated Contrastive Fusion (AECF), a single light-weight layer that (i) adapts its entropy coefficient per instance, (ii) enforces monotone calibration across all modality subsets, and (iii) drives a curriculum mask directly from training-time entropy. On AV-MNIST and MS-COCO, AECF improves masked-input mAP by +18 pp at a 50% drop rate while reducing ECE by up to 200%, yet adds 1% run-time. All back-bones remain frozen, making AECF an easy drop-in layer for robust, calibrated multimodal inference.

link.title: Robust and Sparse Group Dynamic Causal Modeling via Student-t Parametric Empirical Bayes and Nonlocal Priors

entry.content:
Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) estimates directed effective connectivity, while parametric empirical Bayes (PEB) supports group inference using subject-specific posterior summaries. Standard PEB relies on Gaussian models and continuous shrinkage, making it sensitive to atypical estimates and unable to distinguish negligible from nonzero effects. We develop a robust and sparse group-DCM extension combining a Student-$t$ likelihood with a spike-and-slab prior using a nonlocal product-moment (pMOM) slab. A normal–gamma representation of the Student-$t$ distribution yields weights that downweight atypical {whitened residual coordinates}. The pMOM slab vanishes at zero, sharpening coefficient selection and yielding inclusion probabilities. {We propagate first-level posterior uncertainty through block-covariance pre-whitening and use a multistart generalized expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm with conditional maximization for mode fitting, followed by parallel-tempering posterior integration for inclusion probabilities. entry.title: SGD Provably Prioritizes a Shortcut Spurious Feature in the XOR Model

link.title: SGD Provably Prioritizes a Shortcut Spurious Feature in the XOR Model

entry.content:
Neural networks are known to be susceptible to over-reliance on spurious correlations. However, the precise mechanism by which models exploit shortcut features is not fully understood, and algorithms to mitigate this behavior rely on as yet unjustified assumptions about the learned representations. In this work, we provide the first end-to-end theoretical characterization of spurious feature learning for two-layer ReLU neural networks trained by online minibatch SGD on the logistic loss. We consider data drawn from the high-dimensional Boolean hypercube with a quadratic signal function (namely XOR) and a linear spurious correlation. We show that SGD learns the spurious feature first, and exponentially fast. Moreover, the optimization dynamics couple the spurious and signal features, with a stronger spurious component inhibiting signal feature learning. Our analysis reveals precise phase transitions in the learning dynamics. In the first phase, alignment between the signs of the spurious feature and second-layer weight drives rapid growth of the spurious feature. In the second phase, large majority group margin slows learning and the signal feature remains suppressed. When the spurious correlation is maximally strong, we show theoretically that the spurious feature dominates even at the sample complexity threshold where XOR would be learned in isolation (i.e., if the spurious feature was absent). In contrast, when the correlation strength is constant, we provide preliminary evidence that the model can eventually learn the XOR signal, although the spurious feature is not forgotten.

entry.title: Scalable Estimation and Inference for Varying Coefficient Expectile Regression with Streaming Data

link.title: Scalable Estimation and Inference for Varying Coefficient Expectile Regression with Streaming Data

entry.content:
Nonparametric expectile regression methods face new challenges from streaming data, where retaining the full dataset for batch processing becomes increasingly impractical. In this paper, we develop a scalable nonparametric expectile regression framework for varying coefficient models. We estimate the coefficient functions online via functional stochastic gradient descent with Polyak–Ruppert averaging in a product reproducing kernel Hilbert space, requiring only gradient information and one pass over the data. For this online estimator, we establish non-asymptotic error bounds, prove its optimal nonparametric convergence rate under the proposed step-size schemes, and derive its Berry–Esseen bound for pointwise asymptotic normality. To perform online inference for the varying coefficient expectile regression models, we propose a multiplier bootstrap procedure that perturbs the stochastic gradients with independent random weights and recursively constructs bootstrap trajectories. We establish the bootstrap consistency of the online inference procedure, yielding asymptotically valid pointwise confidence intervals. Simulation studies and a real data application confirm the performance of the proposed methods.

entry.title: Self-Distillation is Optimal Among Spectral Shrinkage Estimators

link.title: Self-Distillation is Optimal Among Spectral Shrinkage Estimators

entry.content:
Self-distillation has emerged as a promising technique for improving model performance in modern machine learning systems. We develop the statistical foundations of self-distillation in high-dimensional linear regression by introducing and analyzing a broad class of estimators, namely spectral shrinkage estimators. We consider both spiked and general covariance matrices. For the former, we establish that when the covariance has $s$ distinct spikes, $s$-step self-distillation achieves optimal prediction among spectral shrinkage estimators, outperforming well-known estimators in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, we show that $s$ steps are necessary for optimality: any $(s-k)$-step distilled estimator is strictly suboptimal for $1 \leq k \leq s$. For general covariance matrices, we show that self-distillation approaches the optimal limiting prediction risk among continuous spectral shrinkage estimators as the number of distillation steps increases. We further develop a generalized cross-validation procedure for selecting the distillation parameters from data and establish an asymptotic oracle guarantee for the resulting estimator. We also study a federated approach where multiple data centers share spectral shrinkage estimators and a common server seeks to aggregate them to achieve optimal performance. In this case, we find that the best local rule again takes the form of self-distillation, though it differs from the optimal rule when data are hosted centrally on a single server. Together, our results explain why self-distillation improves predictive performance and provide a broader statistical framework that connects it to classical shrinkage-based methods.

entry.title: Simple Extensions of Single-Objective Acquisition Functions and Hedge Strategies for Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization

link.title: Simple Extensions of Single-Objective Acquisition Functions and Hedge Strategies for Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization

entry.content:
Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) is commonly approached through specialized acquisition functions or scalarization schemes designed to explicitly account for trade-offs among non-preferential objectives. In this work, we show that such complexity might be unnecessary. We propose a framework that extends standard single-objective acquisition functions directly to the multi-objective setting through a hypervolume-based methodology. We further extend hedge strategies for acquisition functions, which are typically used only in single-objective optimization, to the multi-objective regime. Our approach requires minimal modification to existing Bayesian optimization pipelines and avoids the need for bespoke multi-objective formulations. We demonstrate how a broad class of commonly used single-objective acquisition functions and hedge strategies can be adapted in a principled manner to handle multiple objectives, while preserving their intuitive interpretation and computational efficiency. Empirically, we evaluate the proposed methods across a range of synthetic and real-world multi-objective benchmarks. Despite their simplicity, our extensions consistently match or outperform more complex state-of-the-art MOBO methods in terms of optimization performance and sample efficiency. These results suggest that effective multi-objective Bayesian optimization can be achieved by reusing and carefully extending well-established single-objective acquisition strategies, offering a simpler and more flexible alternative to existing approaches.

entry.title: Smooth Concordance Metrics for Survival Models

link.title: Smooth Concordance Metrics for Survival Models

entry.content:
Concordance indices are widely popular metrics for assessing the ability of predictive survival models to discriminate underlying risk levels. However, these statistics have also been criticized for using only the rank orderings of the model’s predicted risk scores and being insensitive to important model features, such as the addition of strong predictor variables into the model. In this paper, we address these limitations by developing smooth concordance metrics that model the underlying risk discrimination probabilities as continuous functions of the predicted risk score differences, where the shapes of these functions are estimated from the observed data. As a result, these smooth concordance metrics assess model performance across the entire range of possible risk score differences, allowing one to identify specific scenarios where the candidate model performs especially well or better than other models. Simulations show that the proposed smooth concordance metrics provide more detailed information about risk discrimination performance and are much more sensitive to the addition of meaningful predictors. We apply these methods to compare predictive survival models for cancer recurrence.

entry.title: Smooth Piecewise Cutting for Neural Operator to Handle Discontinuities and Sharp Transitions

link.title: Smooth Piecewise Cutting for Neural Operator to Handle Discontinuities and Sharp Transitions

entry.content:
Neural operators have achieved strong performance in learning solution operators of partial differential equations (PDEs), but their inherently continuous representations struggle to capture discontinuities and sharp transitions. Existing approaches typically approximate such features within continuous function spaces, often requiring increased model capacity and high-resolution data. In this work, we propose Cut-DeepONet, a two-stage training framework that explicitly models discontinuities while reducing learning complexity. Our approach reformulates the problem via a lifting strategy, partitioning the domain into smooth subregions while representing discontinuities as boundaries in a higher-dimensional space. This separation aligns the operator learning task with the inductive bias of neural networks and avoids directly approximating discontinuities. An additional network predicts input-dependent discontinuity locations for unseen inputs, which are then used to guide the neural operator in generating smooth components within each region. Experiments on benchmark PDEs show that Cut-DeepONet outperforms state-of-the-art methods, even when trained on low-resolution datasets. The method excels on problems with discontinuities and sharp transitions, while using fewer trainable parameters. Our results highlight the benefits of changing the representation of operator learning rather than increasing model complexity.
